facts.claim: "Don't You Give Up On Me Yet" is track 2 on Jonah Kagen's six-song Black Dress EP, released November 22, 2024 on Arista Records.
Jonah Kagen is the credited composer of the song, and the track runs about 3:17.
Black Dress was recorded and produced by Kagen himself while he travelled in his Airstream trailer.
Kagen says he wrote the song entirely from a perspective of desperation, and that the title line is someone begging another person not to give up on them.
Kagen said the lead vocal took about three takes, and he sang it all the way through.
The song was previously unreleased before the EP. It is described as a slowly building strummer with campfire intimacy that casts Kagen as a man on the edge, alone and running on fumes.
Kagen described Black Dress as the first part of a project that is a snapshot of his emotional experience at the time, with songs meant to feel present rather than reflective.
A music video for the song was listed as released on November 29, 2024.
The EP's lead single "God Needs The Devil" went viral and reached number one on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart.
Kagen grew up in Savannah, Georgia, and began playing guitar at age six. He later went to Cornell, where he built a TikTok following. His song "Broken" went viral and led Arista to sign him in 2021.

research.lineage: Kagen's music sits in acoustic, guitar-driven indie folk with a pop sensibility, and his 2024 Black Dress EP was recorded DIY-style in a converted Airstream.

draft:
"They quit on me in Georgia," Jonah Kagen sings on **Don't You Give Up On Me Yet**, and the next line is the one that cuts: they quit on him while telling him "men don't quit." It's a small, bitter irony set inside a song about running on empty, and it explains why the plea in the title lands so hard. The narrator has been abandoned by people who preached endurance at him. Now he's asking one last person to practice what they wouldn't.

Kagen has said he wrote the song entirely from a place of desperation, with the title line as someone begging another person not to give up on them. The lyrics never dress that up. The opening finds him alive "somehow," four nights without sleep, seeing ghosts in the dew. Then the road takes over: backroads, an emptying tank, tires "seeing the miles," a desert where the road is ending. It's a familiar set of images, but Kagen uses them plainly, as a man narrating his own breakdown in real time.

What keeps the song from self-pity is the chorus's honest split. "God knows I'm the one who made the mess," he admits, then immediately: "But I'm fucked up, and they left me for dead." Guilt and grievance sit in the same breath, and neither cancels the other. He knows he got himself burned. He also knows people walked away when he got sick. The song doesn't ask you to decide who's right. It asks you to hold both, the way he has to. And the line about "some last thread I found in you" makes the stakes clear. This isn't a love song so much as a rope thrown from a ditch.

The sound matches that bareness. A strummed acoustic guitar and a simple bass line sit under a steady kit, hi-hat ticking, at a moderate tempo with a quiet push of urgency. The mix is clean and dry, with little reverb, so the voice stays close. Kagen's singing is slightly raspy and mid-range, a single voice with no harmonies to soften it. He has said the lead took about three takes, sung all the way through, and it shows: the delivery is earnest rather than polished, closer to the campfire intimacy the EP was praised for than to radio sheen.

That fits the record's making. Kagen recorded and produced the Black Dress EP himself, travelling in his Airstream, and called it a snapshot of his emotional state, songs meant to feel present rather than reflective. This one feels present. It's acoustic indie folk with a pop sense of where a hook should fall, and the hook is just the request, repeated until it sounds less like a line and more like breathing.

You stay with it because it lets you hear what asking for help sounds like from someone who's been told asking is weakness.
